vignette:
**Case Vignette: Robert M.**

Robert is a 54-year-old married forester who has been coming to see me for the past four weeks. He is a tall, broad-shouldered man with calloused hands and a quiet, deliberate way of speaking. He sits forward in his chair, elbows on his knees, as if bracing himself. He describes himself as someone who has always been steady, reliable, "the one people call when things go wrong." But for the last fourteen months, he has felt like a stranger in his own life.

The event that changed everything happened on a clear October afternoon. Robert was operating a feller buncher in a dense stand of old-growth pine. He had done this work for thirty years. He knew the machine’s rhythm, the sound of its hydraulics, the way the ground felt beneath its tracks. That day, his crew was thinning a section near a logging road. A younger crew member, a man named Derek, had been instructed to stay back and mark trees. But Derek had moved into the cutting zone to retrieve a dropped radio. Robert never saw him. The machine’s arm swung, and a falling tree caught Derek across the legs. The sound—Robert still hears it. Not the machine, not the breaking wood, but the silence afterward. Then the screaming.

Derek survived. He lost his right leg below the knee. Robert visited him in the hospital once. Derek’s wife was there. She said, "He’ll be okay. He doesn’t blame you." Robert has not been able to look Derek in the eye since. He has not returned to that forest. He cannot drive past the logging road without his chest tightening and his hands going numb.

In the months that followed, Robert stopped going to work. At first, he took sick leave. Then he told his supervisor he was "taking a break." His wife, Linda, found him sitting in the dark in the living room at 3 a.m., staring at nothing. He told her he was fine. He told everyone he was fine. But he stopped sleeping. When he does sleep, he dreams of the tree falling in slow motion, of Derek’s face, of the wet sound of impact. He wakes with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, convinced he has just killed someone.

He has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. At the grocery store, he watches people’s feet. He scans parking lots for dropped objects. He cannot be around power tools. Last month, his brother asked him to help split firewood. Robert picked up the maul, looked at the log, and felt a wave of nausea so intense he had to sit down. He told his brother he had the flu. He has not told anyone the truth—that he is terrified of his own hands, of what they might do again.

He avoids all reminders. He no longer drives the back roads. He deleted every photo on his phone that showed trees. He stopped watching the news because a story about a logging accident sent him into a panic attack that lasted forty minutes. Linda has tried to talk to him, but he shuts down. He says, "You don’t understand. I did this. I did this to him." He cannot separate intention from outcome. He replays the moment constantly—what he should have seen, what he should have done differently. He has told me, "I was the expert. I was supposed to be the one who kept everyone safe. I failed."

Physically, he feels on edge all the time. His shoulders are perpetually tight. He has developed a tremor in his left hand that comes and goes. He has lost fifteen pounds because food feels irrelevant. He drinks more than he used to—three or four beers most nights, sometimes whiskey—to quiet the thoughts. It helps for an hour, maybe two. Then the thoughts come back, sharper.

Robert is a man who built his identity on competence and control. He was the one who could read a forest, predict its dangers, protect his crew. Now he cannot trust himself. He told me last session, "I used to know who I was. Now I’m just the guy who ruined someone’s life." He is not suicidal, but he has said he sometimes wishes he could "just disappear." He has no energy for hobbies, no interest in the future. He lives in the past, in that single moment, over and over again.

He is here because Linda made the appointment. He came because he did not know what else to do. He sits in my office with his hands clasped, his jaw tight, and he tells me he does not deserve to feel better. But he is still coming. And that, I think, is the only thing he still trusts—the act of showing up.
